records.our_prose: Lavender has very low fertility needs and is one of the few plants you can harm by feeding. A single inch of compost worked in at planting, or one application of a slow-release fertilizer for the season, is plenty. Over-fertilized plants put on lush foliage at the expense of flowers and fragrance and become more prone to disease and winter injury.

records.our_prose: Central and south Florida are hard country for lavender, and the honest guidance is to keep expectations low. UF/IFAS is clear that lavender is a Mediterranean plant that grows best in Florida's cooler seasons and that the state's high humidity brings fungal root rot. Across the peninsula it is a container or raised-bed plant, not a landscape perennial: plant in sharply drained mix, give afternoon shade against the intense sun, mulch the crown in winter against cold wet soil, keep air moving, and choose only heat- and humidity-tolerant types such as Spanish lavender or the hybrid Phenomenal. Common English lavender reliably fails. In central Florida (zone 10) a well-tended container plant may persist for a few years before declining; in the deep south (zone 11) lavender is genuinely marginal and best treated as a short-lived, cool-season container novelty. Where it flowers, the flush comes in the cooler half of the year, roughly spring into summer.

records.our_prose: Across the Mid-Atlantic Piedmont and Coastal Plain, English lavender is comfortably hardy in both zone 7 and zone 8, so cold is not the constraint it is farther north. The real test here is the region's humid summer: NC State's own profile of the species names root rot from overwatering and leaf spot as the main threats. Plant on a raised, sharply drained mound in full sun, water sparingly once established, and space plants generously for airflow, the same discipline growers rely on across the humid Southeast. Set plants out in spring after the last frost and do the hard cut back the month after bloom fades, never in fall.

records.our_prose: In Utah's Dixie high desert, lavender is a desert-strong perennial: English lavender is hardy well below zone 8, to about zone 5, so winter cold is not this region's real constraint. What matters here is the opposite of a humid-belt cell: this crop thrives in the heat, summer temperatures are not a problem, and established plants are genuinely drought-tolerant, and St. George's alkaline, fast-draining soil is close to lavender's native Mediterranean hillside ground. Give it full sun, lean alkaline soil with sharp drainage, and only occasional deep water once established. Establish plants in the shoulder season, spring or fall, per USU Extension's Suggested Vegetable Planting Dates for Utah.

records.our_prose: Lavender is almost always started from a nursery transplant or from softwood cuttings taken after bloom, not from seed. English lavender does not come true from seed and germination is slow and variable (roughly 100 to 200 days from seeding to a plantable size), so named cultivars are propagated vegetatively. To raise it from seed anyway, cold-stratify the seed for three to six weeks (moist, in the refrigerator) to improve and even germination, then surface-sow at about 70°F since light aids germination, starting indoors roughly 10 weeks before the last frost; expect slow, erratic emergence.

records.our_prose: To dry lavender, cut stems as the first buds open, gather them into small bundles of 50 to 100 stems secured with a rubber band, and hang them upside down in a cool, dark, well-ventilated place. Once dry, strip the buds and store them in a sealed, opaque container away from light and air, which fade the color and scent.
source_names: CSU Extension Fact Sheet 7.245 (Growing Lavender in Colorado)
records.source_context: Harvest the lavender stems in the morning hours when the oils are the most concentrated and when approximately 50 percent of the flower buds have opened. Use a sickle or pruning shears to cut stems as long as possible. Form bundles of 50 to 100 stems and secure them with rubber bands (Figure 5). Rubber bands will contract when the stems dry out.
